strengths: The proposed MMEarth-Bench addresses a critical gap in Earth Observation (EO) research by providing a globally distributed, multimodal dataset with 12 aligned modalities across 5 distinct environmental tasks.

The use of Africa as a dedicated geographic test split provides a realistic, principled, and challenging setting for evaluating out-of-distribution geographic generalization, highlighting actual spatial biases in field data collection.
The benchmarking is exceptionally thorough, evaluating 8 distinct pretrained models (ranging from RGB-only to complex multimodal transformers) and training baselines across different data regimes.
The proposed Test-Time Training with MultiModal Reconstruction (TTT-MMR) is model-agnostic and consistently improves downstream performance over joint training.
The introduction of geographic batching (TTT-MMR-GEO) is a clever, domain-specific inductive bias that significantly improves adaptation performance on the long tail of target distributions.
The appendix is incredibly detailed (64 pages), containing extensive raw results, dataset statistics, modality importance studies, and a clear guide for practitioners.
weaknesses: Inference latency is a notable bottleneck for the proposed method. As shown in Table A.8, TTT-MMR-Geo increases the inference time from under 0.01 seconds per sample to nearly 1.0 second per sample, which may limit real-time or very large-scale global deployments.

The evaluation lacks direct comparison with other established test-time training or test-time adaptation methods designed for multimodal or multi-task setups, focusing primarily on a comparison against the Joint Training (JT) baseline.

The modality reconstruction decoders are very lightweight and simple (linear/bilinear upsampling). While this keeps the parameters to adapt small, the paper does not extensively analyze if more expressive decoders could yield better representation adaptation signals.

strengths: High-Quality and Novel Dataset: The paper introduces MMEarth-Bench, a comprehensive global multimodal Earth Observation (EO) benchmark spanning five key environmental tasks with 12 aligned modalities. It addresses a significant gap in the evaluation of multimodal foundation models.

Systematic and Real-World Evaluation: The authors evaluate 8 diverse pretrained models under low-data regimes and geographic shifts. This thorough benchmarking yields valuable insights, such as the fact that globally pretrained models still struggle heavily with geographic generalization.

Innovative Test-Time Training Approach: The proposed TTT-MMR method is model-agnostic and elegantly repurposes test-time multimodal inputs as self-supervised auxiliary reconstruction targets. This allows any pretrained model to exploit all available test modalities even if it was not pretrained on them.

Geographic Batching for TTA: Introducing geographic batching (TTT-MMR-Geo) is a highly intuitive and effective design choice for geospatial data. It acts as an excellent trade-off between specialization and regularization, and shows significant performance improvements on long-tail/rare samples.

Rigorous Validation and Exemplary Documentation: The paper is exceptionally thorough, backed by a detailed 64-page appendix containing extensive ablation studies, modality importance analyses, raw data tables, and an interactive visualization tool.
weaknesses: Limited Geographic Cross-Validation: The geographic domain shift experiments are restricted to holding out Africa as the test set. While highly justified by the lack of field measurements in Africa, evaluating leave-one-continent-out (e.g., South America or Asia) would significantly strengthen the claims of robust global adaptation.

Computational Overhead of Test-Time Training: Table A.8 in the appendix reveals that TTT-MMR-Geo requires 0.36 to 0.91 seconds per sample, which is roughly a 100x slowdown compared to a standard forward pass (<0.01 seconds). This substantial computational overhead should be discussed more prominently as a limitation in the main text, especially given the scale of global Earth observation data.

Requirement of Joint Training (JT): To apply the proposed test-time training, the model must be trained from scratch (or refinetuned) with the auxiliary task modality decoder. It cannot be applied directly to arbitrary, off-the-shelf finetuned models. Discussing this constraint would clarify the deployment requirements of the method.

strengths: Introduction of MMEarth-Bench, a comprehensive global multimodal Earth Observation (EO) benchmark covering five crucial nature/environmental tasks (biomass, soil nitrogen, soil organic carbon, soil pH, and species occurrence) across 12 aligned modalities.

Carefully designed evaluation protocol incorporating both random splits and a dedicated geographic test split (Africa) to test out-of-domain generalization under domain shift, reflecting realistic challenges in remote sensing.

Comprehensive benchmark evaluating eight recent foundation and supervised models, showing valuable insights (e.g., that simple multimodal models trained from scratch remain very competitive given sufficient training data).

Novel Test-Time Training with MultiModal Reconstruction (TTT-MMR) method, which creatively repurposes auxiliary modalities available at test time as self-supervised reconstruction targets to adapt the encoder parameters on the fly without updating the task decoder.

Introduction of TTT-MMR-Geo, which leverages recursive spatial partitioning (k-d tree) for geographic batching. This physically intuitive design provides a great trade-off between regularization and local specialization, showing significant improvements on long-tail/rare target distributions.
Exceptionally thorough appendix containing meticulous details on dataset generation, hyperparameter setups, linear probing comparisons, raw numerical tables, and statistical significance tests.
weaknesses: Test-time adaptation introduces a significant computational overhead. As shown in Table A.8, TTT-MMR-Geo (5 iterations) is roughly 100x to 400x slower than a standard forward pass. While acceptable for many offline geospatial pipelines, this constraint on inference speed is a notable practical limitation.

The modality decoder is kept extremely simple (a linear layer or 1x1 convolution after bilinear upsampling) to prevent test-time overfitting. However, this design might fail to capture highly non-linear relationships between the input latent space and complex target modalities (such as precipitation or temperature), potentially limiting the quality of the gradient feedback.

The proposed pipeline relies on a Joint Training (JT) phase prior to Test-Time Training. This means users cannot perform TTT directly out-of-the-box with off-the-shelf pretrained foundation models unless they first train the auxiliary modality heads on the downstream source training set, which slightly limits the immediate plug-and-play capability.

strengths: Introduction of MMEarth-Bench, a highly valuable and diverse multimodal benchmark featuring 12 modalities across 5 environmental tasks, with explicit geographic splits (Africa) to evaluate out-of-distribution generalization.
Comprehensive evaluation of 7 diverse state-of-the-art geospatial pretrained models under different low-shot settings (5%, 50%, 100% data) and geographic domain shifts.

A novel and practical test-time training method (TTT-MMR) that leverages auxiliary modalities as reconstruction targets to adapt the encoder at test time, which is model-agnostic and does not require modifications to the encoder architecture.
The concept of geographic batching (TTT-MMR-GEO) is highly intuitive and naturally exploits the spatial autocorrelation of Earth observation data to balance specialization and regularization.
Very detailed supplementary material with extensive descriptions of data generation, raw results for multiple seeds, and qualitative modality reconstruction visualizations.
weaknesses: High computational overhead of the proposed TTT method at inference time. According to Table S.8, TTT-MMR-GEO increases the inference time by roughly 50x to 100x compared to a standard forward pass, which might limit its applicability for real-time global monitoring.

Lack of comparison to unimodal TTA baselines. For example, comparing against a TTT baseline that only reconstructs the input modality (e.g., adapting TTT-MAE to the Earth observation setting) would help isolate the exact benefit of using *multimodal* reconstruction.

The sensitivity of the method to test-time batch sizes is not thoroughly explored, which is critical since online test-time adaptation often operates under stream-like scenarios with very small or single-sample batches.
The requirement of having all 12 modalities available at test time can be a deployment bottleneck in terms of data collection latency and storage, which should be discussed as a practical limitation.

strengths: Fills a crucial gap in Earth Observation (EO) and geospatial machine learning by introducing MMEarth-Bench, a highly diverse, multimodal (12 modalities) benchmark containing realistic downstream environmental tasks with explicit random and geographic splits.
Comprehensive evaluation of 7 recent pretrained model architectures (covering RGB, multispectral, and multimodal inputs) across various low-resource data budgets (5%, 50%, and 100% training data).

Presents a novel and model-agnostic adaptation strategy, Test-Time Training with MultiModal Reconstruction (TTT-MMR), which creatively leverages all available modalities at test time as self-supervised reconstruction targets, bypassing compatibility constraints of the original encoder.
The introduction of TTT-MMR-GEO, using recursive spatial partitioning (k-d tree batching) to guide regional specialization, is highly intuitive and well-suited for georeferenced geospatial data.
Excellent reproducibility and transparency with thorough documentation, exact details of Google Earth Engine dataset generation, code snippets, and an interactive dataset explorer tool.
weaknesses: Limited comparison to existing state-of-the-art Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) or Source-Free Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (SFUDA) baselines beyond Joint Training (JT). Comparing against general TTA methods on the classification task (Species) or a standard self-supervised TTA (e.g., reconstruction of masked inputs) would strengthen the methodological claims.

Significant computational overhead introduced at test-time. Table S.8 shows a transition from 0.007s to 0.910s (a >100x slow-down) per sample for DINOv3-Sat. This latency trade-off is a critical practical deployment concern and should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

The modality reconstruction decoder is highly simplified (mostly linear layers). While computationally efficient, it remains unclear if a slightly more expressive decoder (e.g., a lightweight CNN/MLP) would provide a cleaner adaptation signal or lead to overfitting during TTT.

strengths: Introduction of MMEarth-Bench, a valuable multimodal benchmark dataset with 12 diverse modalities across 5 environmental monitoring tasks, designed with both random and geographic test splits (Africa) to systematically evaluate out-of-distribution generalization.

Extensive benchmarking of 7 state-of-the-art geospatial foundation models (ranging from RGB-only to multispectral and multimodal), highlighting the persistent challenges of geographic generalization in remote sensing.

Proposal of TTT-MMR and TTT-MMR-GEO, a model-agnostic test-time training framework that leverages multimodal reconstruction as an auxiliary task, demonstrating consistent and statistically significant performance improvements on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets.
Excellent reproducibility with comprehensive supplementary materials detailing the dataset statistics, data collection protocols, and raw experiment results across three random seeds.
weaknesses: The proposed TTT method is not fully test-time adaptation (TTA) in the traditional sense, as it requires a Joint Training (JT) phase where the encoder and modality decoders are trained together on the downstream training set. This limits its applicability to fully frozen, black-box off-the-shelf models where the training code or source data is unavailable.

Lack of comparison with existing test-time adaptation (TTA) baselines. While the paper correctly points out that TENT is designed for classification, other regression-compatible TTA methods or simple parameter-update baselines (such as adapting LayerNorm/BatchNorm parameters using auxiliary tasks or pseudo-labeling) should be compared to validate the necessity of the proposed multi-modal reconstruction loss.

The modality reconstruction decoder is a simple linear layer, resulting in highly blurry and simplified reconstructions (as visualized in Figure S.16). It is unclear whether such poor reconstructions provide a meaningful semantic adaptation signal or if they primarily act as a form of unstructured regularization.

High computational overhead at test time: Table S.8 shows that TTT-MMR-GEO increases the inference time per sample by more than 100x (e.g., from 0.007s to 0.910s for DINOv3 Sat). This significantly limits its practicality for global-scale Earth Observation applications where processing efficiency is critical.

Small dataset sizes for the soil property tasks (e.g., Soil N has only 3,787 training tiles and 232 geographic test tiles). These small sample sizes can lead to high variance in the regression metrics (R2), making it harder to draw robust conclusions.
